newsitem.title: GEORGIA: Shevardnadze backs off on Russian troop pullout.
newsitem.headline: Shevardnadze backs off on Russian troop pullout.

text.p: Georgian President Eduard Shevardnadze on Monday urged caution in deciding the future of 1,500 Russian peacekeepers in his former Soviet republic.
The troops patrol a buffer zone between Georgia and its breakaway province of Abkhazia.

Some 10,000 people were killed in a 1992-93 separatist war between Abkhazia and the Tbilisi government, and at least 150,000 ethnic Georgian refugees have still not been able to return to the province.

"A categorical insistence on the withdrawal of Russian forces in the conflict zone could inflame the situation, and real symptoms of this have already appeared," Shevardnadze said in a weekly radio interview.

His comment appeared to be a clear step back from Tbilisi's earlier demands that the Russian peacekeepers, serving under the auspices of the post-Soviet Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), must leave the buffer zone unless they agree to a more intensive peacekeeping mandate. The current mandate expires on Thursday.

The latest CIS summit, held in Moscow in March, decided that the peacekeepers should police more of Abkhazia, which has been effectively outside Tbilisi's control since 1993, and help to repatriate refugees who had fled the region.

Russia has flatly rejected the demand, citing Abkhaz objections, despite warnings from Tbilisi that Moscow might also have to give up three military bases it has in Georgia in addition to the peacekeepers.
Shevardnadze has the right to give the go-ahead for the force to stay. He said parliament would have to be consulted but suggested the force might stay on indefinitely without a new mandate.
"If the forces leave of their own accord, then of course we will not stop them. That is their right," he said.
Analysts say the change in mood in Tbilisi had been caused by fears of a new war in Abkhazia if the peacekeepers left.
Shevardnadze said Western leaders had also cautioned him against forcing the Russian peacekeepers out.
During a recent visit to the United States and talks with United Nations Secretary General Kofi Annan, the Georgian leader insisted on the creation of a multinational peacekeeping force for Abkhazia.
But Shevardnadze has conceded that without the consent of the separatists, which is most unlikely, the idea looks unrealistic. Abkhaz leader Vladislav Ardzinba has rejected the proposal.
U.N.-sponsored peace talks in Geneva last week also brought little progress.
Georgia offers Abkhazia strong autonomy within a federal state. Abkhazia says it will only agree to a union state in which it would be an equal member.
Tbilisi says that is just a smokescreen which would give Abkhazia the right to tear up the agreement at any time and declare full independence.
